description: I am a solo developer who is proficient in programming in Python, specifically in AI libraries such as PyTorch and NumPy. My main skills are in digital signal processing and machine learning.
summary:
I created a AI-powered application that detects irregular heart rhythms in astronauts, called arrhythmias, that are currently in space. The challenge was to create a health monitoring software tool to detect issues in astronauts and help them manage it, so my tool monitors their heart rhythms and predicts whether it is currently dangerous and abnormal so that space stations can be alerted to stop streneous activity and rehydrate for electrolytes if needed, before the rhythm turns life-threatening. 

I developed this tool because astronauts face conditions like microgravity in space, which leaves fluid filling up in their chest and changing the size and electrical stability of their heart. In addition, radiation, stress, and imbalanced hydration can interfere with normal heart rhythms in space. Therefore, the tool calibrates to each astronaut's resting heart baseline and predicts which arrhythmia they have, if any, to maximize accuracy across genders and ages.
details:
The project uses a digital signal processing pipeline to retrieve records from the MIT BIH database on PhysioNet, and process them into clean, filtered signals and frequency-spectrums so they can be used to train a Convolutional Neural Network AI model. The record contains a signal showing the patient's heart rhythm over time (waveform) for 30 minutes on an EKG. Retrieving the record required using the Python library wfdb, while processing it required using NumPy. I trained the model using the Python library PyTorch. The trained model was meant to be able to predict if an arrhythmia was present and which arrhythmia was present in a new patient's record it has not seen before.

After training the model, I wrote a calibration script where the model was briefly fine-tuned on the unseen patient's resting EKG baseline and heart rhythm, as different astronaut's have different baselines depending on gender, age, and fitness. This was a major benefit because it allowed my model to generalize across different genders and ages instead of memorizing patterns for a single type of astronaut and overfitting.

One major factor I considered was that the dataset was severely imbalanced as there were significantly more "normal" patient records than one with arrhythmias, so I decided to cap the number of records in that category I would train the model on by randomly selecting a handful from each patient. That way, the model learns patterns across different patients while not overfitting the normal category.

Explanations of the system architecture, code snippets I wrote, and more information about the challenges faced is in my GitHub README and .md files.
